headline: FTC wants stores to reveal when data sets your price

sources.title: Personalized pricing: Why some pay more than others
FTC moves to make retailers disclose use of 'personalized pricing'
FTC Proposes Enforcement Policy Statement on Personalized Pricing (Skadden)
FTC targets online pricing based on shoppers' personal data (video, KHOU 11)

chunks.text: Two people can look at the same product online and see two different prices. This is called [[personalized pricing]]. [[Retailers]] use [[personal data]] to {{size up}} each shopper and estimate how much that person is [[willing]] to pay. If the system thinks you will {{pay up}}, it can {{mark up}} the price just for you. Another shopper may see a lower price for the same item. Most people never know, so they cannot {{opt out}}.

verbs.correct: To judge someone carefully before acting
verbs.wrong: To pack a customer's order for shipping
verbs.why: A boxer sizes up his opponent before the first punch, and a landlord sizes up a new tenant during the visit. Retailers size up each shopper with personal data to estimate how much that person will pay.

verbs.correct: To give money, even when you do not want to
verbs.wrong: To return money that someone lent you
verbs.why: A driver pays up when the parking fine arrives, and a tenant pays up when the landlord knocks for the rent. If the system thinks a shopper will pay up, it can raise the price for that person.

verbs.correct: To raise the price of something
verbs.wrong: To write a review of a product
verbs.why: A cafe marks up bottled water in summer, and a hotel marks up rooms during a big festival. Stores can mark up the price for a shopper who seems willing to pay more.

verbs.correct: To choose not to be part of something
verbs.wrong: To have no more of a product to sell
verbs.why: You can opt out of a company's marketing emails, and a student can opt out of the school trip. Most shoppers cannot opt out of personalized pricing because they never know it is happening.

chunks.text: The Federal Trade Commission wants that to change. On August 19, 2026, the [[agency]] {{put forward}} an [[enforcement]] [[policy statement]] on personalized pricing and asked the public to {{weigh in}}. The [[comment period]] ran until September 18. Under the [[proposal]], a company would have to tell shoppers when personal data is setting their individual price. A company that hides the [[practice]] could be breaking the law against unfair or [[deceptive]] practices. That would let the FTC {{crack down on}} stores that stay quiet.

verbs.correct: To suggest a plan for others to consider
verbs.wrong: To delay something until a later time
verbs.why: A coach puts forward a new training plan, and a neighbor puts forward an idea for the block party. In August 2026 the FTC put forward an enforcement policy statement on personalized pricing.

verbs.correct: To give your opinion on a topic
verbs.wrong: To make money from a situation
verbs.why: Parents weigh in on the new school schedule, and fans weigh in on a team's new logo. The FTC asked the public to weigh in, and the comment period ran until September 18.

verbs.correct: To start dealing strictly with a problem
verbs.wrong: To admit you were wrong and stop arguing
verbs.why: A city cracks down on illegal parking, and a school cracks down on cheating during exams. Under the proposal, the FTC could crack down on stores that hide the use of personal data in pricing.

chunks.text: The agency has been studying these tools [[for some time]]. In July 2024 the FTC ordered eight pricing-technology companies to {{hand over}} information about how their systems work. The study that followed was published in January 2025. It {{tracked down}} at least 250 [[clients]] of those eight companies, including [[grocery]] retailers. The software, [[in other words]], is not a rare [[experiment]]. It has reached the stores where many people buy their food.

verbs.correct: To give something to someone in charge
verbs.wrong: To share printed papers with a group
verbs.why: A driver hands over his license to the police officer, and a passenger hands over her passport at the border. In July 2024 the FTC ordered eight pricing-technology companies to hand over information about their systems.

verbs.correct: To find something after a careful search
verbs.wrong: To say no to an offer or a request
verbs.why: A librarian tracks down a rare book for a reader, and a mechanic tracks down the cause of a strange noise. The study published in January 2025 tracked down at least 250 clients of those eight companies.

chunks.text: What kind of data feeds these systems? The list is long: precise location, [[browser history]], shopping [[behavior]], [[demographics]] and [[credit history]]. Even your mouse movements can {{give away}} clues about you. Once the software has {{figured out}} your limit, the price follows. The proposal would not end the practice. If it takes effect, people will at least {{find out}} when their data is setting the price. Then they can decide whether to buy or {{walk away}}.

verbs.correct: To show something without meaning to
verbs.wrong: To agree to something after resisting
verbs.why: A nervous smile gives away a surprise party, and a child's face gives away who ate the cookies. Even a shopper's mouse movements can give away clues about how they shop.

verbs.wrong: To write information on a form
verbs.why: A student figures out a hard math problem, and a couple figures out the fastest route to the airport. Once the software has figured out a shopper's limit, the price follows.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To be tricked by something false
verbs.why: A patient finds out the results of a blood test, and a fan finds out the concert date from a poster. If the proposal takes effect, shoppers will find out when their data is setting the price.

verbs.correct: To leave instead of accepting a deal
verbs.wrong: To try a product before you buy it
verbs.why: A buyer walks away when the car dealer refuses to lower the price, and a worker walks away from a job offer with bad hours. Shoppers who know the price is personalized can decide whether to buy or walk away.

mainIdea.s: The FTC wants stores to tell shoppers when personal data is used to set their price. Companies that hide the practice could be breaking the law.
mainIdea.why: In August 2026 the agency put forward an enforcement policy statement, and a company that stays quiet could face the law against unfair or deceptive practices.

mainIdea.s: The FTC has proposed a ban on stores using personal data to set individual prices. Companies that keep doing it anyway could be breaking the law.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the proposal would not end the practice. It only asks stores to tell shoppers when personal data is setting their price.

mainIdea.s: Eight grocery chains agreed to show every shopper the same price after a customer lawsuit. The stores will also delete all the data they collected.
mainIdea.why: No lawsuit or agreement is reported. The FTC put forward a proposal about telling shoppers, and it asked the public to weigh in.

lines.text: Have you heard of personalized pricing? Two people open the same page, and they see two different prices for the same product.
For the exact same thing? How does the store decide who pays more?
It uses personal data to {{size up}} each shopper. If the system thinks you'll {{pay up}}, it can {{mark up}} the price just for you.
So the same thing costs me more? [[That's highway robbery]]. What kind of data are we talking about?
Location, browser history, shopping behavior, credit history. Even your mouse movements can {{give away}} clues about how you shop.
My mouse? Then I'll have to [[keep a poker face]] with my cursor from now on.
It won't help. Once the software has {{figured out}} your limit, the price follows.
That sounds like [[a slippery slope]]. Can people say no to it?
Not really. Most shoppers never know it's happening, so they can't {{opt out}}.
Is anyone doing anything about it?
The Federal Trade Commission is. In August it {{put forward}} a proposal and asked the public to {{weigh in}}. Stores would have to tell you when your data is setting your price.
And if a store keeps quiet?
It could be breaking the law, so the FTC could {{crack down on}} it.
How common is this, though? It sounds like a small experiment.
It isn't. Back in 2024 the FTC ordered eight pricing-technology companies to {{hand over}} details about their systems. The study {{tracked down}} at least 250 clients, including grocery retailers.
Grocery stores? [[Buyer beware]], I guess, even when I'm just buying eggs.
The proposal wouldn't end the practice. But at least you'd {{find out}} when it's happening.
[[Better than nothing]]. Then I can decide whether to buy or {{walk away}}.

expressions.def: Used to say that a price is unfairly high
ex: Twelve dollars for a bottle of water? That's highway robbery.
They charged me fifty dollars to change my seat. That's highway robbery.

expressions.def: To hide your feelings so nobody can tell what you are thinking.
ex: She kept a poker face while the boss read her report.
Keep a poker face when they tell you the price, or they'll know you love it.

expressions.def: A first small step that can lead to worse and worse results
ex: Skipping one workout is a slippery slope.
Some parents think one phone app is a slippery slope.

expressions.def: Used to say that shoppers must be careful because sellers may not be fair
ex: The used car looked perfect, but buyer beware.
Cheap tickets online? Buyer beware.

expressions.def: Used to say that a small improvement is still worth having.
ex: The refund was only ten dollars, but it's better than nothing.
A warning label won't fix the problem, but it's better than nothing.
